bib.title: Everything is Connected: Graph Neural Networks

question: What are the key concepts of graph representation learning, and how do GNNs relate to Deep Sets, Transformers and geometric equivariant models?
contributions: A short survey that introduces permutation invariance and equivariance, the three spatial GNN flavours (convolutional, attentional, message-passing), GNNs without an input graph (Deep Sets, Transformers, latent graph inference) and geometric (E(3)-equivariant) GNNs.

limits: Short survey with no experiments; explicitly not a comprehensive overview of GNN layers.
Edge features are deliberately left out of the formalism for clarity.
Expressivity claim (Eq. 10 is all we need) is stated as the author's opinion; existence of a powerful GNN does not mean SGD finds it.
Latent graph inference is only listed by paradigm, not compared.
practices: Choose the GNN flavour (convolutional, attentional, message-passing) by trading expressivity against interpretability, scalability and stability (Section 3).

Use an invariant readout (sum/mean/max over nodes) for graph classification and a shared per-node classifier for node classification; for link prediction classify h_u || h_v plus edge features (Section 3).
When no graph is given, use a fully connected graph (Transformer) for small node counts, or infer the graph (latent graph inference) (Section 4).
For 3D inputs, use E(3)-equivariant layers; use tensor-field style layers when vector features are needed (Section 5).
